I said that public opinion
would prevent them from introducing a resolution which was not founded on proper reason.
And in the same way, public opinion would prevent another chamber of this parliament from refusing to dismiss a trustee who should be dismissed.
I was following the statement of the Prime Minister that they could put another government out of office.

I would not like to argue with the Prime Minister as to constitutional questions, but I must confess that I do not interpret the matter in the way he does. Suppose a government of the day wished to dismiss a trustee. The procedure would be something like this: the government of the day would introduce a resolution to the House of Commons in which cause would be given; that resolution would go to the Senate and if it passed the Senate, the man would be dismissed; if the Senate did not pass it, the man would not be dismissed.

That is
what we thought.

The only thing wrong
with the minister's argument is the fact that these trustees will not be judges. Judges are appointed to interpret the laws passed by parliament. A judge may be impeached and brought to the bar of this house for trial. This is the high court of the nation and we merely delegate our powers to the judges of the land to interpret our laws. In this case we are appointing administrators who are going to administer these railways to the best of their knowledge and ability. We are not going to give them any directions as to how that is to be done; we are not going to pass a statute to say that this, that or the other thing shall be done. They are to be given carte blanche and will act entirely on their own volition. They are in an entirely different position from that occupied by the judges and there cannot be any comparison between the two.

The assent of the Senate to the removal of an officer is quite competent when that officer is appointed by parliament. The general returning officer is appointed by joint address of both houses of parliament. The Auditor General of Canada is responsible to parliament. Parliament delegates powers to the cabinet council; the government of the day is merely a committee of parliament. Parliament has the power to remove these officials which I have mentioned but only by the assent of both houses. In the present case this argument would not apply because the trustees are not to be appointed by both houses, they are to be appointed by the governor in council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Which comprises both houses.

The governor in council is responsible to this parliament. I have no desire to disparage the Senate, as I have heard splendid descriptions of its responsibilities and irresponsibilities. In this instance we are dealing with a money question which comes entirely within the jurisdiction of this house. The Senate has not a word to say. The Senate can reject a supply bill holus bolus but it cannot amend it. When I was a young man this whole issue was brought to the fore in the Quebec legislature. A conflict arose between the cabinet and the legislative council and pandemonium reigned in that province for some time. Responsible government ceased to exist because the lieutenant governor arrogated to himself powers similar to those which we now seek to confer upon the Senate. The result was that the government of that province was sustained for two years by the casting vote of the Speaker. A precedent was established by the removal of the lieutenant governor by the governor in council. He was declared to be merely a federal officer and not a representative of the crown. The then governor general referred the matter to the home authorities who declared that the lieutenant governor of a province was a nominee of the dominion cabinet which had the power to remove him for cause. At the present time we are merely using our prerogatives as members of this house dealing with a money matter. We are appointing trustees to administer public property, and with all due respect to the Prime Minister, I must say that I am amazed at his stating that a government would have to resign office and go to the people merely because an adverse vote had been cast by the Senate.

The hon. gentleman has fallen three times into the same error-in spite of his wide experience in constitutional matters, he has referred to the cabinet as a committee of this house. It is not; it is a committee of parliament. Ever since confederation there has not been a cabinet in which there has not been a member of the second chamber. The hon. gentleman may easily be excused for falling into that error, but if it is corrected, the argument which he advances vanishes immediately. The cabinet is a committee of parliament and I trust it will always remain so.
The question of taxation would not arise in this case unless it so happened that the road did not earn enough to pay the salaries. I think it would be reasonable to assume that if the road did not earn enough to pay its salaries, the trustees would not come to this parliament to ask it to provide money. They are to be employees of the road and the bill is clear on that point. Their salaries are to be paid from the revenues of the road and not from the consolidated fund of Canada. There will be no charge upon the consolidated fund. The only way such a charge could be made would be in the form of an item. I cannot conceive of these trustees coming to this parliament for their salaries when the road had not made sufficient to pay operating expenses and to provide salaries. Usually that point does not arise in connection with companies of this character.
As to the point which I put to the committee a short time ago in connection with the possibility of the government falling by reason of there not being a joint address, I would state that that was predicated upon the fact that the dismissal took place before they came to parliament. Perhaps that point was not sufficiently clear in the minds of those who followed me. Assuming that the government of the day, that is the executive, took the responsibility of dismissing a trustee or trustees and assigned a cause. If, as has been suggested, that is not a true interpretation of the section but rather that the action follows a joint address of parliament, it is obvious that the government would not fall if the Senate did not agree. If the government risked its power-I am trying to make it perfectly clear-by giving notice of a dismissal from employment of John Smith and assigned cause, it is obvious the government has staked its life upon being able to carry through the action which it has initiated. That means a joint address of both houses of parliament and if one house only passes it, it follows that the government has failed.

That would be a matter which should engage the attention of the administration of the day, and when I said that the government would resign, I mean only that a government that I lead would do so. Other governments might take a different view. It is always competent for the leader of the government of the day to take the view that such a situation does not constitute a termination of his office. Hon. gentlemen who have studied political biographies will remember that when Lord Rosefoury resigned, it was thought that he should not have done so. I am merely expressing my personal and independent opinion that if the executive of the day, speaking through the governor in council, passed an order in council dismissing John Smith as a trustee and assigned a cause for so doing, the government then of course must face just what I said a moment ago, the joint support of both houses, that is, the Commons and the Senate, because the statute so provides, and if only one gave its approval, then the government bad failed in the action which was taken by its executive.

about resigning.

No; I was only trying

I mention that merely because the matter depends entirely-and I am sorry my hon. friends have approached it from the wrong angle-on the method of approach. bound one way or the other, but it would be an impossible situation to have a board of trustees or any member of it operating in that way.
But it all comes back to this-and I submit it to the committee with some confidence -if we are to secure the type of business men we require for the purpose of discharging this function, we must do as I have suggested. I do not desire in any sense to belittle the arguments that have been made as to political control of railways and references to public services. The fact is that as between private and public ownership, you must sharply differentiate between ownership and administration. If the public in the narrow sense is to manage and administer the enterprise, disaster is inevitable, but if the administration is to be conducted by those who are skilled and competent, under the same restrictions and with the same supervisions and safeguards as are imposed by shareholders upon their directors and as public ownership, that is the public ownership of a utility, exercises its power to ensure it that security, stability, continuity, efficiency and effectiveness in management and administration that are essential, then I believe we may succeed. But I do not think there is any chance for what I call public ownership if it is to be subject to the pitfalls that arise from purely public administration, and I draw a sharp distinction between holding administration responsible not to the whole body of the public and the delegation of administration of power by the government to the persons selected for that purpose. That has been the experience, at least in other countries. In Germany they have had for a long time a system of public administration. In Australia their railroads were so administered for a time, and it will be remembered that Sir Thomas Tait, then Mr. Thomas Tait, left for Victoria for the purpose of administering the state railways. Each state had a different gauge, so that the cars of one state could not go beyond its boundaries into another.
Many hon. gentlemen know we have had great difficulty in connection with what we describe in no offensive terms as the political effect on governments of the administration of government-owned property. I should like to give the committee an illustration of that because I should think every hon. member would be interested. One of the members of the pension appeal board brought an action against t'he crown for damages for his salary. It will be recalled that the position was abolished in 1930. I daresay hon. members

will remember that by a joint committee we arrived at certain conclusions and they had the result of abolishing the appeal board as then existing. The consequence was that several gentlemen were out of positions; they secured a fiat and brought an action against the crown. This action was dismissed by the exchequer court and by the Supreme Court of Canada. The other day counsel applied for leave to appeal to the privy council. In reading the proceedings and the application I find that counsel said this: After this statute was passed, there was a general election in Canada and as a result of this changed condition, the appellant, not being of the political faith of the new government, did not secure a position under the new administration as he would have had the government of the day been sustained, and others who were of a different faith were more fortunate. That illustrates what counsel will say before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council regarding political matters in a country like this.

one of public ownership but not of public control; the most that one can say is that it is quasi-public control but not public control in the full or any real sense of the word.

Not control of detailed

The operations, I should say, are distinct from the financial aspect. Of course, in one sense everything connected with the railways must depend upon the finances; but the budget means receipts and expenditures, and I submit that you cannot have public control of any railways unless you have the entire financial affairs of those railways subject to review by parliament. Assuming that the railways are obliged to come to parliament only in so far as it is necessary to make good deficits and the like, these deficits bear a relationship to original expenditures, as well as to original receipts; and to ascertain whether or not such expenditures have been justifiable, and whether the receipts are what parliament had a right to anticipate, involves of necessity a full review. The minister says that we can discuss all these things anyhow. I say that if we can discuss them, to make our discussion of any value we ought to have the final say. Discussion means nothing if as a result of it parliament cannot voice its opinion to effect one way or the other.

But parliament can discuss these things as much as it has ever done. According to my interpretation of the clause, parliament can in the future discuss such matters as extensively as it has done in the past, although what my right hon. friend says is true, namely, that the loss would already have been incurred. But that has always been so; we have always dealt with the budget only in so far as deficits, betterments and additions have been concerned. Under my right hon. friend's government as under this, that has been the method pursued. My absolute conviction is that under this clause we have as full power as we have ever had to go into any matter we wish to discuss, but I do not think it would be wise to make the operating budget of the railways subject to approval of parliament. That would be carrying parliamentary interference to an extent unheard of in the past.
Will the government be still obliged to authorize capital expenditures?

Yes; that is distinctly
indicated in the next sentence.
The situation with respect to additional capital expenditures will remain as it is.
Yes.

It seems to
me that the government and parliament are really on the horns of a dilemma in dealing with this matter. My difference with the minister is perhaps most simply stated by citing the actual facts, in the words that seem to be most applicable. I think it is a mistake to talk of public control when parliament is deliberately handing over the control of the budget to three trustees who are independent entirely of the House of Commons. I think we might as well say that the government are of the view that public ownership and public control in the full sense of the word are not possible; that the most the government are prepared to concede is that there can be public ownership with a degree of quasi public control. If the minister feels that it will embarrass the situation to have the entire budget brought before parliament, the ministry being held responsible, I will not press the matter further. My own view however is that the Minister of Railways should be continued as such and should be answerable to parliament for the action of the trustees. He should as minister, as a member of the cabinet, review the situation of the national railways in its entirety, and the budget of the railways in its entirety should be brought to parliament; whether to be discussed in detail or not, whether to be discussed in a special committee or in the committee of the whole house, are matters for the government to decide. If you are going to have public control, I think it is necessary that some minister of the crown should take responsibility for the budget framed by the trustees, and being clothed with the necessary authority the government should be prepared to stand or fall as it is supported or not supported.

I wonder if the minister has considered fully the wording of this section? I understand that his intention is that the items mentioned here, that is, income deficits, interest on obligations outstanding in the hands of the public, capital expenditures and refunding or retirement of maturing securities, shall be submitted to parliament. The minister is perhaps more familiar than I with the act, but let me point out that the act provides for the issuance of securities for equipment purposes without the approval of parliament. That is a capital expenditure which may be made without the

approval of parliament. I mention this because it seems to me the section is none too clear in requiring that these expenditures shall be submitted to parliament. It is worded rather vaguely, the effect being that they shall be submitted by the trustees to the Minister of Finance for the consideration of the governor in council prior to presentation to parliament. Section 28 of the act provides for certain capital expenditures which do not have to be submitted to parliament but which may be passed by the governor in council. Section 30 provides that after parliament has authorized expenditures on equipment to the extent of twenty-five per cent of the cost, the company may make equipment issues for the remaining seventy-five per cent. Under subsection 4 of section 28 equipment certificates and other obligations may be issued without the intervention of parliament. I think the section should be worded a little more clearly so as to provide definitely that these things shall be all submitted to parliament, rather than having the nebulous provision that they shall be submitted to the governor in council prior to presentation to parliament.

The hon. member is right as to section 30 of the act. For the information of the committee, I shall read that section. It is:
Where parliament has .authorized expenditures on equipment to the extent of twenty-five per cent of the cost of such equipment, the company may make or cause to be made one or more equipment issues for the remaining seventy-five per cent of such cost.
My hon. friend is slightly in error. In the past these matters had to come before parliament. It is quite true the railway could borrow seventy-five per cent of the cost but it had first to submit to parliament the twenty-five per cent. This is known as the Philadelphia plan and is followed by all the railways on the continent in the purchasing of equipment. Let us say that a railway desires to buy $1,000,000 worth of equipment. They would get twenty-five per cent of the cost from their shareholders-in this case the parliament of Canada-and they would go out and borrow the remaining seventy-five per cent of the cost in the form of equipment trust bonds. These were usually sold in the United States but during the past year, because of the financial situation in the United States and the financial condition of the Canadian National Railways, these have had to be taken up entirely by parliament. I am afraid that for some time to come the amounts needed for equipment will have to be considered in parliament in the estimates of the Minister 53719-291
of Finance just the same as other additions and betterments. But in any event, twenty-five per cent of the cost would have to be approved of by parliament before the railways could go out and borrow the other seventy-five per cent. At the present time there is no chance at all of the Canadian National Railways borrowing money on their own guarantee. As my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce points out, in any event they would have to come here for twenty-five per cent of the cost. I do not think that clause 12 lessens the powers of the Canadian National Railways.

Would the minister just look at the section. I am suggesting that after the word "submitted" there be inserted the words " to parliament". There would then be no question at all as to these matters having to be submitted to parliament. The words "prior to presentation to parliament" would be struck out. I think that would make the section much clearer and would leave no necessity for implication.

I would point out that irrespective of the act, these matters have to come to parliament. The Minister of Finance has to provide the money and the only way he can do that is by an estimate. The money must be voted by parliament, so the matter must come to parliament.
As I understand it, seventy-five per cent of the cost is raised by equipment issues without coming to parliament.

They must first come to
parliament for twenty-five per cent.

seventy-five per cent without first getting the twenty-five per cent.

Section 30 of the act is
an enabling clause. Where parliament has authorized expenditures on equipment to the extent of twenty-five per cent of the cost, the company may authorize issues for the remaining seventy-five per cent. Subsection 4 of section 28 refers to equipment certificates or obligations in any form intended to be issued to the public. Under that section they are issued by the governor in council and not by parliament. I contend that this section could be drafted ini such a way as to require the submission of these things to parliament instead of stating in an indirect way that they shall be submitted to the Minister of Finance for the consideration of the governor in council prior to presentation to parliament.

A statement was given to the House of Commons last week showing the gross revenues of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific Railways for the first eleven reporting periods of 1933 as compared with the corresponding periods of 1932. The fact that the Canadian National Railways returns showed a decrease of 23 per cent as compared with 1932 and those of the Canadian Pacific Railway a 17 per cent decrease has led certain editorial writers to draw unwarranted deductions. One Toronto newspaper said yesterday:

"On the face of things the Canadian National Railways is getting the worst of the cooperation deal."
The cooperative economies have had nothing to do with the fluctuations in the amount of decrease on the two major Canadian railway systems. The Canadian National management is continuously watchful of the traffic and other interests of the system and there has been no diminution in its efforts to safeguard its business. The fluctuations to which attention has been drawn are no greater than previous fluctuations which were in favour of the Canadian National. The relative traffic situation of the two properties varies from time to time in accordance with changes in the crop conditions and trade conditions in the territories respectively served by the carriers. The explanation of the present swing is to be found in two major factors. The first is that the Canadian Pacific gross earnings are at present receiving a stimulus from a comparatively good crop in 1932 in southern Saskatchewan and Alberta, in which territory that system is the chief transportation agency. For the previous three years that territory had suffered from crop failures. The second condition affecting the relative showing at this time is the falling off in traffic between the United States and Canada and the reduction in United States traffic passing through the dominion, the business disturbance which accompanied the "banking holiday" having accentuated this decline in recent weeks. The Canadian National, by reason of the location of its lines in Canada and the United States, is a larger factor in business of this character than the Canadian Pacific. The earnings of the Canadian National Railways therefore reflect more closely the conditions which have prevailed in the United States and international traffic. In the working out of cooperative measures between the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific Railways, yon may be assured that the best interests of the Canadian National system will be fully protected.
That was a telegram which, in so far as its contents are concerned, was unsolicited by me. I merely drew to Mr. Hungerford's attention this editorial which was a very severe one along the line mentioned, and asked him for an explanation. This is his explanation which is a very full one. 23. Where the execution of an order, or the carrying out of a decision of a tribunal, involves the doing of any act which by any statute requires the leave, sanction, assent or approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners, or where in the opinion of the presiding officer of a tribunal composed of not more than three members the public interests involved are of sufficient importance to warrant it, no order made by a tribunal shall be operative without the concurrence of the presiding officer and his formal written assent, and on such concurrence and assent having been given, no such leave, sanction, assent or approval of the said board will be required.
Perhaps that was a little difficult to follow, and I might explain it in a few sentences. Originally it was provided tihat in a case with which the Board of 'Railway Commissioners had a right to deal in the ordinary course of events, or in a case where the chairman thought the public interest was involved, he could veto the decision of the other members. It was drawn to my attention, I think particularly by the hon. member for Dauphin, that the chairman should not be in a position to overrule the other four members if they differed from him. I thought this was a reasonable attitude, so this change has -been made. In a case where, in the ordinary course of events, the Board of Railway Commissioners would be consulted, the chairman of the arbitral tribunal, who is also the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, can veto the decision if he wishes, because he is acting in the dual capacity of chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners and chairman of the tribunal. In the second place, when there are three members of the tribunal and the chairman considers the matter in the public interest he can overrule the other two members. He has that power because as chairman of the board he is supposed to be, and I think has been and is at present, more familiar with railway questions and with the public interest as it bears upon those questions than the other members may be. So when there are three members of a tribunal the chairman can overrule the other two if he considers it in the public interest that he should do so. Then, in an arbitral tribunal consisting of five members-because as my hon. friends know there are cases in which two other members may be brought in-where it is only a matter of public interest the chairman cannot overrule the other four members; if three of the other four take a certain position he has not the power to overrule them.

. . . the economies to be realized eventually by consolidation-and I believe there will be very substantial economies-will come through making it unnecessary to provide as much new capital as might otherwise be necessary. That is one economy.
The other economies which can be lumped in one item, are labour and material, less of both being needed, probably-particularly labour. In fact, the only way economies can be made to any extent in railroad service is by the use of fewer employees, and with that would always go the use of some less labour. Our figures show that the wages paid for labour constitute about sixty per cent of our total operating expenses, and material about forty per cent. speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to give some relief to soldier settlers and to civilian purchasers of land under the Soldier Settlement Act. It is proposed that the interest accruing in the year 1932 shall be entirely remitted. Section 73 provides that any settler or purchaser whose contract was njade prior to January 1, 1933, and who make*
Soldier Settlement Act

payments enuring the fiscal years 1933-34, 1934-35, and\1935-36 on arrears or instalments due between April 1, 1933, and March 31, 1937, inclusive, shall have his account credited with an additional amount equal to such payment. Section 74 deals with what is known as the three thousand British family scheme. Heretofore settlers brought to Canada under that scheme did not receive the benefits of certain remedial legislation that was passed from time to time. Section 74 provides that the effect of this statute shall be applied to those settlers, provided, of course, that the imperial government takes such action as will permit us to take that course. As hon. members, I think, know, while the Dominion government provided the land, the imperial government provided stock and equipment. Thus there will be a division of the loss in proportion to the amount involved for each government. Generally speaking, the interest oi the Canadian government in this scheme is 62J per cent and the balance is taken care of by the imperial government. This is the way in which the loss would, generally speaking, be apportioned, if the imperial government takes appropriate action to bring their settlers within the scope of this enactment.
